questions.stem: What does rotating a magnet inside a coil of wire generate?

options.text: an induced alternating voltage in the coil
options.explanation: Rotation changes the field and induction delivers voltage.
The rotating field reverses each half turn, so the output alternates.

options.text: a magnetic force on the coil
options.explanation: That is the motor effect; generation is induction.
The coil gains voltage, not permanent magnetism.

questions.stem: Which arrangement also generates electricity by rotation?

options.text: winding more wire but never moving anything
options.explanation: Turns scale the effect; motion is still required.

options.text: rotating a coil of wire inside a magnetic field
options.explanation: Both 6.16 arrangements generate.

options.text: holding a coil still inside a steady field
options.explanation: No change means no induction.

options.text: sliding a magnet along beside the coil without entering
options.explanation: The field through the coil must change.

questions.stem: Why is the generator's output voltage alternating?

options.text: the magnet switches off twice per turn
options.explanation: The magnet stays magnetised; the field direction swings.
Heating is irrelevant to the alternation.

options.text: the rotation reverses the field change every half turn
options.explanation: Each half turn flips the induced polarity.
Resistance is not the cause of alternation.

questions.stem: Which change increases the size of a generator's induced voltage?

options.explanation: Slower rotation gives a smaller voltage.

options.text: using fewer turns on the coil
options.explanation: Fewer turns reduce the summed voltage.
A weaker field gives a smaller voltage.
Faster change of field gives larger induced voltage.

questions.stem: A hand-cranked generator lights a lamp dimly at one crank speed. To brighten the lamp the student should:

options.text: crank faster to induce a larger voltage
options.explanation: More speed, more voltage, brighter lamp.
Slower cranking dims the lamp further.

options.text: remove turns from the generator coil
options.explanation: Fewer turns induce less voltage.
The lamp needs the circuit to glow at all.

questions.stem: State the two rotation arrangements that generate electricity.
questions.modelAnswer: Rotating a magnet inside a coil of wire, or rotating a coil of wire inside a magnetic field.

questions.stem: State three factors that change how large a generator's induced voltage is.
questions.modelAnswer: The speed of rotation, the strength of the magnetic field, and the number of turns on the coil.

questions.stem: Explain why the induced voltage of a spinning-magnet generator changes direction twice per revolution.
questions.modelAnswer: Each revolution carries the magnet's field through the coil one way, then the other: the field threading the coil grows, peaks, falls, and reverses as the magnet turns. The induced voltage follows the field change, so its polarity flips at the half-turn points — twice per revolution.

questions.stem: A bicycle dynamo drives a lamp; the rider speeds up. Describe the change in the lamp's brightness and explain it by the generator factors.
questions.modelAnswer: The lamp brightens. The faster wheel spins the generator's magnet faster, so the field through the coil changes more quickly and the induced voltage grows — a larger voltage drives a larger current through the lamp, making it brighter.

questions.stem: What does a dynamo deliver to the external circuit?

options.explanation: The output is one-way by design.

options.text: direct current in one direction only
options.explanation: The split-ring commutator rectifies the output.
That is the alternator's slip-ring output.
The dynamo is a working generator.

questions.stem: What does the split-ring commutator do in a dynamo?

options.explanation: The commutator reroutes; it never amplifies.

options.text: disconnects the circuit twice per turn
options.explanation: It swaps contacts; it does not break the circuit twice per turn as its purpose.

options.text: swaps the external connection every half turn
options.explanation: The swap folds the alternation into one-way flow.
The coil keeps spinning; the contacts follow it.

questions.stem: The voltage induced IN the dynamo coil itself is:

options.text: direct current, because it is a dynamo
options.explanation: The DC label describes the delivery, not the coil voltage.
The spinning coil induces a real voltage.
The induced voltage oscillates with the rotation.

options.text: alternating, as in any rotating generator
options.explanation: Rectification happens outside the coil, at the contacts.

questions.stem: Which component would you fit to keep the ALTERNATING output of a generator unchanged?

options.explanation: Slip rings pass the alternating output through untouched.
That rectifies the output into DC.
Extra field changes size, not the AC character.
Axle length is electrically irrelevant.

questions.stem: The rotation of a dynamo speeds up. The lamp it feeds:

options.explanation: The induced voltage grows with speed.

options.text: glows brighter, with current still flowing one way
options.explanation: Bigger induced voltage, same one-way delivery.
The commutator keeps the delivery one-way.
More rotation means more voltage, not none.

questions.stem: State the component that converts a generator's alternating output to direct.
questions.modelAnswer: A split-ring commutator swaps the connection every half turn, delivering direct current.

questions.stem: State what slip rings deliver that a split-ring commutator does not.
questions.modelAnswer: Slip rings deliver the alternating current unchanged, while the commutator delivers one-way direct current.

questions.stem: Explain why the dynamo's output current never reverses even though the coil's induced voltage does.
questions.modelAnswer: Each half turn, the split-ring commutator swaps which brush connects to which coil end. When the coil's induced voltage reverses, the external connections have just been swapped too, so the reversal inside is cancelled outside: the circuit always sees the same polarity, and the current flows one way throughout.

questions.stem: A bicycle lamp is fed first by a slip-ring alternator, then by a split-ring dynamo of the same coil and magnet. Compare the currents in the lamp circuit.
questions.modelAnswer: With slip rings the lamp current alternates direction every half turn at the same frequency as the wheel. With the split-ring dynamo the current always flows the same way through the lamp, pulsing in size but never reversing. The peak sizes match — the same coil and magnet induce the same voltages — only the delivery differs.
